<script>
  // Restore the saved color scheme preference, or
  // enact the browser preference if "automatic", 
  // without expecting DOM load to have completed.
  //
  // Also restore any saved readingmode and ToC display preferences.
  function initializeReadingPreferences() {
    let saved_theme = localStorage.getItem("ar5iv_theme") || "automatic";
    if (saved_theme === "automatic") {
      if (window.matchMedia("(prefers-color-scheme: dark)").matches) {
        saved_theme = "dark";
      }
    }
    if (saved_theme == "dark") {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "dark");
    } else {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "light");
    }

    const tocDisplay = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_toc_display');
    if (tocDisplay) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-toc-display", tocDisplay);
    }
    const readingMode = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_reading_mode');
    if (readingMode) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-reading-mode", readingMode);
    }
    // Pre-apply spinout-banner dismissal here, before the banner paints, so it
    // never flashes in only to be hidden later by the deferred arxiv-header.js.
    // Key matches arxiv-header.js: "arxiv-banner-dismissed:" + data-banner-name.
    if (localStorage.getItem('arxiv-banner-dismissed:spinout-nonprofit')) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-banner-dismissed", "");
    }
  }
  // Run as soon as JS starts, to minimize repainting
  initializeReadingPreferences();
</script>

<li class="ltx_tocentry ltx_tocentry_bibliography"><a href="#bib" title="In Understanding the Fine-Grained Knowledge Capabilities of Vision-Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_title">References</span></a></li>
<li class="ltx_tocentry ltx_tocentry_appendix"><a href="#A1" title="In Understanding the Fine-Grained Knowledge Capabilities of Vision-Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_title"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_ref">A </span>Full Results</span></a></li>
<li class="ltx_tocentry ltx_tocentry_appendix"><a href="#A2" title="In Understanding the Fine-Grained Knowledge Capabilities of Vision-Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_title"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_ref">B </span>Evaluation</span></a>
<ol class="ltx_toclist ltx_toclist_appendix">
<li class="ltx_tocentry ltx_tocentry_subsection"><a href="#A2.SS1" title="In Appendix B Evaluation ‣ Understanding the Fine-Grained Knowledge Capabilities of Vision-Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_title"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_ref">B.1 </span>Fine-grained classification</span></a></li>

</ol></li>

</ol></nav>
</nav>

<article class="ltx_document ltx_authors_1line">
<h1 class="ltx_title ltx_title_document">Understanding the Fine-Grained Knowledge 
<br class="ltx_break">Capabilities of Vision-Language Models</h1>
<div class="ltx_authors">
<span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Dhruba Ghosh
</span></span>
<span class="ltx_author_before">  </span><span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Yuhui Zhang
</span></span>
<span class="ltx_author_before">  </span><span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Ludwig Schmidt
</span></span>
<span class="ltx_author_before">  </span><span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Stanford University
</span></span></div>

<div id="abstract1" class="ltx_abstract"><h6 class="ltx_title ltx_title_abstract">Abstract</h6>
    
<p id="abstract1.1" class="ltx_p">Vision-language models (VLMs) have made substantial progress across a wide range of visual question answering benchmarks, spanning visual reasoning, document understanding, and multimodal dialogue. These improvements are evident in a wide range of VLMs built on a variety of base models, alignment architectures, and training data. However, recent works show that these models trail behind in traditional image classification benchmarks, which test fine-grained visual knowledge. We test a large number of recent VLMs on fine-grained classification benchmarks and identify potential factors in the disconnect between fine-grained knowledge and other vision benchmarks. Through a series of ablation experiments, we find that using a better LLM improves all benchmark scores equally, while a better vision encoder disproportionately improves fine-grained classification performance. Furthermore, we find that the pretraining stage is also vital to fine-grained performance, particularly when the language model weights are unfrozen during pretraining. These insights pave the way for enhancing fine-grained visual understanding and vision-centric capabilities in VLMs.</p>
  
</div>
<div id="p1" class="ltx_para">
<table id="p1.1" class="ltx_tabular ltx_align_top">
<tbody class="ltx_tbody">
<tr id="p1.1.1" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="p1.1.1.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left"><span class="ltx_rule" style="width:0.0pt;height:24.0pt;--ltx-bg-color:black;display:inline-block;"></span></td></tr>
</tbody>
</table>
</div>
<section id="S1" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">1 </span>Introduction</h2>

<div id="S1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Recent advances in vision-language models (VLMs), which integrate vision encoders with large language models (LLMs), have demonstrated increasingly sophisticated capabilities in interpreting and reasoning about visual content <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">Alayrac et al., 2022</a>; <a href="#bib.bib34" title="" class="ltx_ref">Team et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib28" title="" class="ltx_ref">OpenAI, 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib26" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liu et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib44" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2024b</a>)</cite>. These models can perform complex tasks such as open-ended visual question answering, document understanding, and multimodal dialogue <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib35" title="" class="ltx_ref">Goyal et al., 2017</a>; <a href="#bib.bib43" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yue et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib36" title="" class="ltx_ref">Mathew et al., 2021</a>; <a href="#bib.bib28" title="" class="ltx_ref">OpenAI, 2023</a>)</cite>. Despite these advances, a crucial question remains: How well do VLMs perform on fine-grained visual perception tasks, and how can we improve their performance?</p>
</div>
<figure id="S1.F1" class="ltx_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_1"><img src="2602.17871v1/pull_9.png" id="S1.F1.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_figure_panel ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:494/182;" width="494" height="182" alt="Refer to caption"></div><div class="ltx_flex_break"></div><div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_2"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2602.17871v1/all_ablations_1.svg" id="S1.F1.g2" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_figure_panel ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:242/145;" width="242" height="145"></object></div><div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_2"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2602.17871v1/all_ablations_average_1.svg" id="S1.F1.g3" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_figure_panel ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:242/145;" width="242" height="145"></object></div></div>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 1: </span><span id="S1.F1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Overview.</span> <span id="S1.F1.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">(Top)</span> We investigate the fine-grained classification capabilities of vision-language models (VLMs), a crucial yet often overlooked aspect that underpins higher-level understanding and reasoning. <span id="S1.F1.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">(Bottom)</span> Through 22 systematic ablation experiments on key model components and training strategies (left), we identify the factors that drive fine-grained classification performance in VLMs (right).</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Fine-grained visual recognition—the ability to distinguish between visually similar categories—
requires models to focus on subtle distinguishing features while maintaining robustness to intra-class variations in pose, lighting, and background. While traditional vision encoders like CLIP <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">Radford et al., 2021</a>)</cite> and DINO <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">Caron et al., 2021</a>)</cite> have demonstrated strong performance on fine-grained classification benchmarks, the performance of newer VLMs has received less attention.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Understanding the fine-grained knowledge capabilities of VLMs is essential because perception serves as the foundation for advanced capabilities such as understanding and reasoning. Real-world applications of VLMs often involve fine-grained, long-tailed distributions where distinguishing between closely related categories is crucial. For instance, if a model fails to identify a mushroom species correctly, it cannot determine whether it is poisonous based on textual knowledge or whether it is safe for consumption. Moreover, insights into the factors influencing fine-grained knowledge acquisition could inform more effective architectures and training strategies for future VLMs.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">In this paper, we first present a comprehensive evaluation of fine-grained visual knowledge in state-of-the-art VLMs, comparing their performance on fine-grained classification benchmarks with their capabilities on general VLM tasks. Specifically, we evaluate 15 VLMs, such as LLaVA <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib26" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liu et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liu et al., 2024a</a>)</cite>, Phi <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib46" title="" class="ltx_ref">Abdin et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, Qwen2-VL <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib44" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2024b</a>)</cite>, Molmo <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib47" title="" class="ltx_ref">Deitke et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, on four fine-grained classification benchmarks, including ImageNet <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib25" title="" class="ltx_ref">Deng et al., 2009</a>)</cite>, Flowers <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">Nilsback and Zisserman, 2008</a>)</cite>, Pets <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">Parkhi et al., 2012</a>)</cite>, and Food <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">Bossard et al., 2014</a>)</cite>, alongside aggregated results from eight general VLM benchmarks such as MMMU <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib43" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yue et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, MathVista <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib42" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lu et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, and MMVet <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib38" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yu et al., 2024</a>)</cite>. Our analysis reveals significant variance in fine-grained classification performance among models with comparable general abilities, suggesting that fine-grained recognition represents a distinct axis of visual intelligence not captured by existing VLM benchmarks. Furthermore, we observe a persistent gap between VLMs and their CLIP-based vision encoders, mirroring previous findings <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib32" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhang et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">Geigle et al., 2024</a>)</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p5" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p5.1" class="ltx_p">To better understand what contributes to fine-grained classification performance in VLMs, we conduct a systematic study examining the role of key model components and training paradigms.
Specifically, we investigate whether VLM components, such as language models and vision encoders, impact classification performance and whether training strategies, such as pretraining or variations in data qualities, influence results.
Through 22 carefully designed ablation experiments, we identify several factors that significantly affect fine-grained knowledge acquisition in VLMs:</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p6" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<ul id="S1.I1" class="ltx_itemize">
<li id="S1.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S1.I1.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Language model (§<a href="#S4.SS2" title="4.2 Base Models ‣ 4 Ablations: Base Models and Training ‣ Understanding the Fine-Grained Knowledge Capabilities of Vision-Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.2</span></a>):</span> Improvements in the base language model enhance performance uniformly across both fine-grained classification and general VLM benchmarks.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S1.I1.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Vision encoder (§<a href="#S4.SS2" title="4.2 Base Models ‣ 4 Ablations: Base Models and Training ‣ Understanding the Fine-Grained Knowledge Capabilities of Vision-Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.2</span></a>):</span> A stronger vision encoder improves fine-grained classification performance but has a limited impact on general VLM benchmarks, particularly in models trained in a two-stage fashion.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.I1.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S1.I1.i3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Pretraining stage (§<a href="#S4.SS3" title="4.3 Training Methods ‣ 4 Ablations: Base Models and Training ‣ Understanding the Fine-Grained Knowledge Capabilities of Vision-Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.3</span></a>):</span> Large-scale pretraining on image-captioning datasets significantly boosts fine-grained classification performance but has a lesser effect on general VLM benchmarks.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.i4" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i4.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.I1.i4.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S1.I1.i4.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Weight updating method (§<a href="#S4.SS3" title="4.3 Training Methods ‣ 4 Ablations: Base Models and Training ‣ Understanding the Fine-Grained Knowledge Capabilities of Vision-Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.3</span></a>):</span> Fine-grained classification performance improves when both the connector between the vision encoder and LLM, as well as the LLM itself, are trained during pretraining, compared to training only the connector.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.i5" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i5.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.I1.i5.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S1.I1.i5.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Data quality (§<a href="#S4.SS3" title="4.3 Training Methods ‣ 4 Ablations: Base Models and Training ‣ Understanding the Fine-Grained Knowledge Capabilities of Vision-Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.3</span></a>):</span> The quality of pretraining and instruction-tuning data has a limited impact on fine-grained classification, particularly when language model weights are frozen during pretraining.</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
</div>
<div id="S1.p7" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p7.1" class="ltx_p">In summary, our study examines fine-grained visual perception in VLMs—an essential yet overlooked aspect of current VLM benchmark evaluations. Through systematic ablations, we identify key factors influencing fine-grained knowledge acquisition in VLMs. These findings offer valuable insights for developing vision-centric VLMs with enhanced visual understanding, improving their effectiveness in real-world long-tail tasks that demand fine-grained recognition.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">2 </span>Related Work</h2>

<div id="S2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Vision-language models and their evaluation.</span>
Vision-language models (VLMs) are a class of models that integrate visual inputs with language models, typically following the LLaVA-based architecture <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib26" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liu et al., 2023</a>)</cite> of three core components:
a vision encoder, a language model, and an MLP connector bridging the two.
These models have achieved strong performance across various multimodal tasks, including visual question answering (VQA), document understanding, and general reasoning <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib26" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liu et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">Dai et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib33" title="" class="ltx_ref">Awadalla et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib44" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2024b</a>)</cite>.
To evaluate VLMs, numerous benchmarks have been developed, such as MMMU <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib43" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yue et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, MathVista <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib39" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2024a</a>)</cite>, and DocVQA <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib36" title="" class="ltx_ref">Mathew et al., 2021</a>)</cite>.
However, these benchmarks primarily assess reasoning and language understanding given visual inputs, while overlooking core vision-centric capabilities such as object recognition and fine-grained classification.
To bridge this gap, in this work we systematically evaluate and analyze VLMs on fine-grained classification, an essential yet underexplored aspect of visual intelligence.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Fine-grained visual classification.</span>
Fine-grained classification is a well-established computer vision task that aims to distinguish between visually similar subcategories within broader object categories, such as bird species <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib27" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wah et al., 2011</a>)</cite>, flowers <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">Nilsback and Zisserman, 2008</a>)</cite>, and pet breeds <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">Parkhi et al., 2012</a>)</cite>.
These benchmarks have played a key role in training and evaluating vision encoders, like ResNet <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">He et al., 2016</a>)</cite>, CLIP <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">Radford et al., 2021</a>)</cite> and DINO <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">Caron et al., 2021</a>)</cite>.
Despite their importance in vision research, recent VLMs have largely overlooked these datasets in their evaluation protocols in favor of visual question-answering.
Since fine-grained classification is critical for real-world applications that involve long-tail distributions and require precise recognition (e.g., medical diagnosis, food safety, and species identification), evaluating VLMs on such benchmarks is essential for understanding their practical usability from a vision-centric perspective, beyond language-centric reasoning tasks.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Evaluation and ablation of VLMs for fine-grained classification.</span>
While recent studies have explored VLM evaluation on fine-grained classification <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib32" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhang et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">Geigle et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, they have been limited in scope, often focusing on just a few models or datasets.
We extend these efforts by evaluating a broader range of VLMs across multiple fine-grained classification benchmarks in a unified multiple-choice format.
Additionally, we go beyond prior work with a comprehensive ablation analysis to identify key factors that impact fine-grained classification performance.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.p4.1" class="ltx_p">Several recent works have investigated the design space of VLMs, analyzing aspects such as model architectures <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">McKinzie et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, training strategies <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib20" title="" class="ltx_ref">Karamcheti et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, and the role of multimodal datasets <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">Gadre et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">Udandarao et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib47" title="" class="ltx_ref">Deitke et al., 2024</a>)</cite>.
However, these studies primarily focus on general benchmarks that are more language and reasoning-focused.
In this work, we investigate how key design choices—including base model selection, pretraining methods, and the composition of pretraining and instruction-tuning data—affect fine-grained classification, providing novel insights into optimizing VLMs for vision-centric tasks.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">3 </span>Evaluation: Fine-grained Classification</h2>

<div id="S3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In this section, we discuss the motivation for evaluating fine-grained classification, describe our benchmarks and evaluation setup, and present our key observations from testing 15 existing VLMs.</p>
</div>
<section id="S3.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.1 </span>Motivation</h3>

<div id="S3.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Fine-grained classification is a fundamental task in computer vision that focuses on distinguishing visually similar subcategories within a broader category (e.g., different bird species or car models) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wei et al., 2021</a>)</cite>.
Many evaluation benchmarks, such as ImageNet <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib25" title="" class="ltx_ref">Deng et al., 2009</a>)</cite> and Flowers <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">Nilsback and Zisserman, 2008</a>)</cite>, have been developed and widely used as standard testbeds for training and evaluating vision encoders.
With the advent of large-scale self-supervised and supervised learning, vision encoders such as CLIP <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">Radford et al., 2021</a>)</cite> and DINO <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">Caron et al., 2021</a>)</cite> achieved near- or superhuman performance on challenging fine-grained classification tasks.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">However, these benchmarks have been overlooked in the evaluation of vision-language models (VLMs).
While recent VLMs like LLaVA <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib26" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liu et al., 2023</a>)</cite> have demonstrated strong capabilities in interpreting visual concepts, their evaluation is typically limited to visual question answering (VQA), such as academic VQA benchmarks like MMMU <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib43" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yue et al., 2024</a>)</cite> and MathVista <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib42" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lu et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, or document understanding tasks like DocVQA <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib36" title="" class="ltx_ref">Mathew et al., 2021</a>)</cite> and TextVQA <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib37" title="" class="ltx_ref">Singh et al., 2019</a>)</cite>.
These benchmarks emphasize reasoning and language processing but lack fine-grained object categories, thereby leaving core vision-centric capabilities largely unexamined.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS1.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Fine-grained classification is crucial for VLMs, as real-world applications often encounter long-tailed distributions that require precise visual knowledge between similar categories.
For example, in daily life, if a blind person asks whether a mushroom is safe to eat, the model must first correctly identify the species before reasoning about its toxicity—misclassifying a deadly destroying angel as an edible white button mushroom could have fatal consequences.
Similarly, in medical diagnosis, failing to distinguish between similar diseases could lead to incorrect treatment and serious health risks.
In self-driving cars, confusing a “stop” sign with a “do not enter” sign—both red with similar shapes—could result in dangerous navigation errors.
Therefore, it is critical for VLMs to excel at fine-grained classification to ensure safety and reliability in real-world scenarios.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.2 </span>Benchmarks</h3>

<div id="S3.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We evaluate the fine-grained visual knowledge of VLMs using four well-established object recognition benchmarks, each focusing on different domains of fine-grained classification:
<span id="S3.SS2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">ImageNet-1K</span> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib25" title="" class="ltx_ref">Deng et al., 2009</a>)</cite>, <span id="S3.SS2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Oxford Flowers-102</span> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">Nilsback and Zisserman, 2008</a>)</cite>, <span id="S3.SS2.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Oxford-IIIT Pet-37</span> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">Parkhi et al., 2012</a>)</cite>, and <span id="S3.SS2.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Food-101</span> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">Bossard et al., 2014</a>)</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">These benchmarks contain 37 to 1,000 distinct classes, making direct evaluation of VLMs in a multiple-choice format—commonly used in VLM training and evaluation—challenging.
To address this, we adopt the methodology of <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">Geigle et al. (2024)</a></cite> to convert these datasets into 5-way multiple-choice questions.
Specifically, for each image, we use an OpenCLIP ViT-L/14 model <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">Schuhmann et al., 2022</a>)</cite> to select the four hardest negative choices based on image-label cosine similarity and combine them with the ground-truth label to form the multiple-choice answers.
We choose OpenCLIP model to avoid biasing the difficulty against VLMs which rely on OpenAI-CLIP <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">Radford et al., 2021</a>)</cite>, SigLIP <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhai et al., 2023</a>)</cite>, or DFN-CLIP <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib49" title="" class="ltx_ref">Fang et al., 2023</a>)</cite> (which are all trained on different datasets than the OpenCLIP model).
This conversion to multiple choice allows us to test VLMs in their native format while preserving much of the difficulty.
For instance, CLIP ViT-L/14-336px <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">Radford et al., 2021</a>)</cite> obtains 75.2% accuracy on the 102-class Flowers-102, which only increases to 78.3% accuracy on our 5-way multiple choice version.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.3 </span>Testing Setup</h3>

<div id="S3.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We evaluate 15 recent VLMs in the 7B–13B parameter range on the converted 5-choice fine-grained classification benchmarks <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib26" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liu et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liu et al., 2024a</a>; <a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chen et al., 2024a</a>; <a href="#bib.bib46" title="" class="ltx_ref">Abdin et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib47" title="" class="ltx_ref">Deitke et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib48" title="" class="ltx_ref">Laurençon et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib45" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hong et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chen et al., 2024c</a>; <a href="#bib.bib44" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2024b</a>)</cite>.
For each VLM, we use the respective default prompt format from VLMEvalKit <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">Duan et al., 2024</a>)</cite> and measure accuracy based on the exact match with the multiple choice options.
For baseline comparison, we evaluate various CLIP models <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">Radford et al., 2021</a>; <a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">Schuhmann et al., 2022</a>; <a href="#bib.bib49" title="" class="ltx_ref">Fang et al., 2023</a>)</cite> in the standard zero-shot setup, where both images and class labels (“A photo of a [class]”) are encoded using CLIP’s image and text encoders.
The top-1 prediction is determined by computing the cosine similarity between image and text embeddings.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS3.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">To assess whether fine-grained classification capabilities are captured by existing VLM evaluation benchmarks, we compare VLM performance on fine-grained classification benchmarks to their average score on eight general VQA benchmarks, such as MMMU <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib43" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yue et al., 2024</a>)</cite> and MathVista <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib42" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lu et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, from VLMEvalKit.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS4" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.4 </span>Results</h3>

<figure id="S3.F3" class="ltx_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_2">
<figure id="S3.F3.fig1" class="ltx_figure ltx_figure_panel ltx_minipage ltx_align_center ltx_align_middle" style="width:159.0pt;"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2602.17871v1/existing_models.svg" id="S3.F3.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_square" style="aspect-ratio:220/220;" width="220" height="220"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 2: </span><span id="S3.F3.fig1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Fine-grained classification compared to general VQA performance across VLMs.</span> Analysis of recent VLMs indicates that fine-grained classification represents a distinct aspect of visual capability that standard VQA benchmarks fail to measure.</figcaption>
</figure></div><div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_2">
<figure id="S3.F3.fig2" class="ltx_figure ltx_figure_panel ltx_minipage ltx_align_center ltx_align_middle" style="width:222.6pt;"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2602.17871v1/vlm_clip.svg" id="S3.F3.g2" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:307/205;" width="307" height="205"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 3: </span><span id="S3.F3.fig2.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Comparison of VLMs with their corresponding CLIP vision encoders in fine-grained classification.</span> While Qwen2-VL-Chat nearly matches the performance of its vision encoder DFN-CLIP, all other VLMs fall significantly behind. This highlights that VLMs have considerable room for improvement in fine-grained classification tasks.</figcaption>
</figure></div></div>
</figure>
<div id="S3.SS4.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Figure <a href="#S3.F3" title="Figure 3 ‣ 3.4 Results ‣ 3 Evaluation: Fine-grained Classification ‣ Understanding the Fine-Grained Knowledge Capabilities of Vision-Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a> shows the relationship between fine-grained classification performance (averaged across our four benchmarks) and general VQA performance (averaged across eight existing VQA benchmarks) for all tested VLMs.
We observe that models with similar performance on general VQA benchmarks exhibit substantial variation in fine-grained classification accuracy.
For example, while CogVLM-Chat <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib45" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hong et al., 2024</a>)</cite> and LLaVA-NeXT-Vicuna-13B <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liu et al., 2024a</a>)</cite> both achieve nearly 48% average accuracy on general VQA benchmarks, their fine-grained classification accuracy differs by 19pp (percentage points)—77.3% for CogVLM-Chat and 58.1% for LLaVA-NeXT-Vicuna-13B.
This large discrepancy indicates that fine-grained classification capabilities are not well captured by existing VLM evaluation benchmarks, highlighting fine-grained classification as a distinct dimension of visual intelligence.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS4.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent"><span class="ltx_inline-block"><svg id="S3.SS4.p2.pic1" class="ltx_picture" height="48.59" overflow="visible" version="1.1" viewBox="0 0 550 48.59" width="550"><g style="--ltx-stroke-color:#000000;--ltx-fill-color:#000000;" fill="#000000" stroke="#000000" stroke-width="0.4pt" transform="translate(0,48.59) matrix(1 0 0 -1 0 0)"><g style="--ltx-fill-color:#404040;" fill="#404040" fill-opacity="1.0"><path style="stroke:none" d="M 0 5.91 L 0 42.68 C 0 45.94 2.64 48.59 5.91 48.59 L 544.09 48.59 C 547.36 48.59 550 45.94 550 42.68 L 550 5.91 C 550 2.64 547.36 0 544.09 0 L 5.91 0 C 2.64 0 0 2.64 0 5.91 Z"></path></g><g style="--ltx-fill-color:#F2F2F2;" fill="#F2F2F2" fill-opacity="1.0"><path style="stroke:none" d="M 1.97 5.91 L 1.97 42.68 C 1.97 44.86 3.73 46.62 5.91 46.62 L 544.09 46.62 C 546.27 46.62 548.03 44.86 548.03 42.68 L 548.03 5.91 C 548.03 3.73 546.27 1.97 544.09 1.97 L 5.91 1.97 C 3.73 1.97 1.97 3.73 1.97 5.91 Z"></path></g><g fill-opacity="1.0" transform="matrix(1.0 0.0 0.0 1.0 21.65 13.78)"><foreignObject style="--ltx-fo-width:36.62em;--ltx-fo-height:1.52em;--ltx-fo-depth:0em;font-size:10pt;" height="21.03" overflow="visible" transform="matrix(1 0 0 -1 0 21.03)" width="506.72"><span class="ltx_foreignobject_container"><span class="ltx_foreignobject_content"><span id="S3.SS4.p2.pic1.1" class="ltx_inline-sectional-block ltx_minipage">
                    
<section id="S3.SS4.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_font_bold ltx_font_italic ltx_title_paragraph" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">Finding 1:</h5>

<span id="S3.SS4.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<span id="S3.SS4.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS4.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">Fine-grained classification represents a distinct aspect of visual capability that current VLM benchmarks fail to adequately measure.</span></span>
</span>
</section>
                  </span></span></span></foreignObject></g></g></svg></span>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS4.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS4.p3.1" class="ltx_p">An important aspect of current VLMs is that they each build on an existing pretrained vision encoder.
This means that with the multiple-choice format, we can directly compare performance between VLMs and CLIP models on traditional classification benchmarks.
Figure <a href="#S3.F3" title="Figure 3 ‣ 3.4 Results ‣ 3 Evaluation: Fine-grained Classification ‣ Understanding the Fine-Grained Knowledge Capabilities of Vision-Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a> compares the fine-grained classification performance of selected VLMs with their corresponding CLIP model baselines, revealing a substantial gap between them.
For instance, Molmo <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib47" title="" class="ltx_ref">Deitke et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, a very recent model which excels on different VQA benchmarks obtains only a 68.4% average accuracy in our multiple choice evaluation setting, while its vision encoder CLIP ViT-L/14 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">Radford et al., 2021</a>)</cite> obtains 86.7%.
Even the best tested model, Qwen2-VL-Chat <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib44" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2024b</a>)</cite>, falls 4.6 points behind its own state-of-the-art DFN-CLIP <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib49" title="" class="ltx_ref">Fang et al., 2023</a>)</cite> vision encoder.
This performance gap underscores the need to analyze different design choices in VLMs to identify key factors that enhance fine-grained classification capabilities.
In the next section, we conduct an ablation study to investigate these factors.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS4.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent"><span class="ltx_inline-block"><svg id="S3.SS4.p4.pic1" class="ltx_picture" height="48.59" overflow="visible" version="1.1" viewBox="0 0 550 48.59" width="550"><g style="--ltx-stroke-color:#000000;--ltx-fill-color:#000000;" fill="#000000" stroke="#000000" stroke-width="0.4pt" transform="translate(0,48.59) matrix(1 0 0 -1 0 0)"><g style="--ltx-fill-color:#404040;" fill="#404040" fill-opacity="1.0"><path style="stroke:none" d="M 0 5.91 L 0 42.68 C 0 45.94 2.64 48.59 5.91 48.59 L 544.09 48.59 C 547.36 48.59 550 45.94 550 42.68 L 550 5.91 C 550 2.64 547.36 0 544.09 0 L 5.91 0 C 2.64 0 0 2.64 0 5.91 Z"></path></g><g style="--ltx-fill-color:#F2F2F2;" fill="#F2F2F2" fill-opacity="1.0"><path style="stroke:none" d="M 1.97 5.91 L 1.97 42.68 C 1.97 44.86 3.73 46.62 5.91 46.62 L 544.09 46.62 C 546.27 46.62 548.03 44.86 548.03 42.68 L 548.03 5.91 C 548.03 3.73 546.27 1.97 544.09 1.97 L 5.91 1.97 C 3.73 1.97 1.97 3.73 1.97 5.91 Z"></path></g><g fill-opacity="1.0" transform="matrix(1.0 0.0 0.0 1.0 21.65 13.78)"><foreignObject style="--ltx-fo-width:36.62em;--ltx-fo-height:1.52em;--ltx-fo-depth:0em;font-size:10pt;" height="21.03" overflow="visible" transform="matrix(1 0 0 -1 0 21.03)" width="506.72"><span class="ltx_foreignobject_container"><span class="ltx_foreignobject_content"><span id="S3.SS4.p4.pic1.1" class="ltx_inline-sectional-block ltx_minipage">
                    
<section id="S3.SS4.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_font_bold ltx_font_italic ltx_title_paragraph" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">Finding 2:</h5>

<span id="S3.SS4.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<span id="S3.SS4.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS4.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">A significant performance gap exists between VLMs and CLIP models in fine-grained classification tasks.</span></span>
</span>
</section>
                  </span></span></span></foreignObject></g></g></svg></span>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S4" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">4 </span>Ablations: Base Models and Training</h2>

<section id="S4.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.1 </span>Experimental Setup</h3>

<div id="S4.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Building on our observational results in Section <a href="#S3" title="3 Evaluation: Fine-grained Classification ‣ Understanding the Fine-Grained Knowledge Capabilities of Vision-Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>, we ablate key differences between models that may contribute to fine-grained classification performance, focusing primarily on base model selection and training methodology.
We build on the LLaVA-1.5 training framework and alignment architecture <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib26" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liu et al., 2023</a>)</cite>.
All models undergo one epoch of pretraining (when applicable) followed by one epoch of finetuning.
We use LLaVA-1.5’s default hyperparameters, including learning rate and batch size, across all experiments.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Fine-grained performance is evaluated as the average score across the four classification benchmarks described in Section <a href="#S3.SS2" title="3.2 Benchmarks ‣ 3 Evaluation: Fine-grained Classification ‣ Understanding the Fine-Grained Knowledge Capabilities of Vision-Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.2</span></a>.
For general VQA performance, we report the average score on three widely-used multiple-choice benchmarks:
MMMU <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib43" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yue et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, MMBench <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib31" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liu et al., 2024b</a>)</cite>, and MMStar <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib41" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chen et al., 2024b</a>)</cite>.
These benchmarks were selected for their domain coverage and widespread adoption in VLM evaluation.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.2 </span>Base Models</h3>

<div id="S4.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Our analysis in Section <a href="#S3" title="3 Evaluation: Fine-grained Classification ‣ Understanding the Fine-Grained Knowledge Capabilities of Vision-Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a> indicates that recent models typically incorporate newer base LLMs, though most continue to use the CLIP ViT-L/14 vision encoder from <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">Radford et al. (2021)</a></cite>.
We investigate how these base model choices specifically impact fine-grained classification performance.</p>
</div>
<section id="S4.SS2.SSS1" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">4.2.1 </span>LLM Choice</h4>

<figure id="S4.F5" class="ltx_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_2">
<figure id="S4.F5.fig1" class="ltx_figure ltx_figure_panel ltx_minipage ltx_align_center ltx_align_middle" style="width:190.8pt;"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2602.17871v1/llm_ablation.svg" id="S4.F5.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:264/176;" width="264" height="176"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 4: </span><span id="S4.F5.fig1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Ablating base LLM, swapping out Vicuna-7B from LLaVA with other LLMs.</span> On average, switching from Vicuna to Qwen2-7B results in a +7.5pp increase in fine-grained performance and a +7.7pp improvement in general VQA performance.</figcaption>
</figure></div><div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_2">
<figure id="S4.F5.fig2" class="ltx_figure ltx_figure_panel ltx_minipage ltx_align_center ltx_align_middle" style="width:190.8pt;"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2602.17871v1/ve_ablation.svg" id="S4.F5.g2" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:264/176;" width="264" height="176"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 5: </span><span id="S4.F5.fig2.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Ablating base vision encoder, swapping out CLIP ViT-L/14 from LLaVA for DFN-CLIP ViT-H/14.</span> We find that switching to DFN-CLIP improves fine-grained performance by +4.5pp and general performance by +1.2pp, given enough pretraining.</figcaption>
</figure></div></div>
</figure>
<div id="S4.SS2.SSS1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS2.SSS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS2.SSS1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Setup.</span>
Using LLaVA-1.5-7B <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib26" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liu et al., 2023</a>)</cite> as our baseline, we ablate the LLM component across different vision encoders and pretraining configurations.
We compare the original Vicuna-7B-1.5 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chiang et al., 2023</a>)</cite> (used in LLaVA) against Qwen2-7B <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib29" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yang et al., 2024</a>)</cite> (used in Qwen2-VL-7B <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib44" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2024b</a>)</cite> and Molmo-7B-D <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib47" title="" class="ltx_ref">Deitke et al., 2024</a>)</cite>), as well as Llama-2-7B <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib30" title="" class="ltx_ref">Touvron et al., 2023</a>)</cite> (Vicuna’s base model) and Qwen2-7B-Instruct (the instruction-tuned variant of Qwen2-7B).</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.SSS1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS2.SSS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS2.SSS1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Findings.</span>
As shown in Figure <a href="#S4.F5" title="Figure 5 ‣ 4.2.1 LLM Choice ‣ 4.2 Base Models ‣ 4 Ablations: Base Models and Training ‣ Understanding the Fine-Grained Knowledge Capabilities of Vision-Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a>, replacing Vicuna-7B with Qwen2-7B substantially improves performance across all configurations, with average gains of +7.5pp (percentage points) on fine-grained benchmarks and +7.4pp on general VQA benchmarks.
The instruction-tuned Qwen2-7B-Instruct shows similar improvements (+7.5pp and +8.1pp, respectively).
Llama2-7B, the non-instruction-tuned base of Vicuna, yields modest improvements, though the downstream implications of using a model without instruction tuning remain unclear.
Notably, all our trained models—including the lower-performing Vicuna-based VLMs—consistently produce multiple-choice responses in the correct format.
This suggests that performance differences in fine-grained classification stem from improved knowledge about the presented options rather than better format adherence.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.SSS1.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent"><span class="ltx_inline-block"><svg id="S4.SS2.SSS1.p3.pic1" class="ltx_picture" height="48.59" overflow="visible" version="1.1" viewBox="0 0 550 48.59" width="550"><g style="--ltx-stroke-color:#000000;--ltx-fill-color:#000000;" fill="#000000" stroke="#000000" stroke-width="0.4pt" transform="translate(0,48.59) matrix(1 0 0 -1 0 0)"><g style="--ltx-fill-color:#404040;" fill="#404040" fill-opacity="1.0"><path style="stroke:none" d="M 0 5.91 L 0 42.68 C 0 45.94 2.64 48.59 5.91 48.59 L 544.09 48.59 C 547.36 48.59 550 45.94 550 42.68 L 550 5.91 C 550 2.64 547.36 0 544.09 0 L 5.91 0 C 2.64 0 0 2.64 0 5.91 Z"></path></g><g style="--ltx-fill-color:#F2F2F2;" fill="#F2F2F2" fill-opacity="1.0"><path style="stroke:none" d="M 1.97 5.91 L 1.97 42.68 C 1.97 44.86 3.73 46.62 5.91 46.62 L 544.09 46.62 C 546.27 46.62 548.03 44.86 548.03 42.68 L 548.03 5.91 C 548.03 3.73 546.27 1.97 544.09 1.97 L 5.91 1.97 C 3.73 1.97 1.97 3.73 1.97 5.91 Z"></path></g><g fill-opacity="1.0" transform="matrix(1.0 0.0 0.0 1.0 21.65 13.78)"><foreignObject style="--ltx-fo-width:36.62em;--ltx-fo-height:1.52em;--ltx-fo-depth:0em;font-size:10pt;" height="21.03" overflow="visible" transform="matrix(1 0 0 -1 0 21.03)" width="506.72"><span class="ltx_foreignobject_container"><span class="ltx_foreignobject_content"><span id="S4.SS2.SSS1.p3.pic1.1" class="ltx_inline-sectional-block ltx_minipage">
                      
<section id="S4.SS2.SSS1.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_font_bold ltx_font_italic ltx_title_paragraph" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">Takeaway 1:</h5>

<span id="S4.SS2.SSS1.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<span id="S4.SS2.SSS1.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS2.SSS1.Px1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">Stronger language models consistently improve performance across both fine-grained classification and general VQA benchmarks.</span></span>
</span>
</section>
                    </span></span></span></foreignObject></g></g></svg></span>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS2.SSS2" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">4.2.2 </span>Vision Encoder Choice</h4>

<div id="S4.SS2.SSS2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS2.SSS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS2.SSS2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Setup.</span>
Most evaluated VLMs, including the LLaVA series and Molmo, use OpenAI-CLIP ViT-L/14-336px <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">Radford et al., 2021</a>)</cite> as their vision encoder.
However, Qwen2-VL <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib44" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2024b</a>)</cite> uses DFN-CLIP ViT-H/14-378px <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib49" title="" class="ltx_ref">Fang et al., 2023</a>)</cite>, which demonstrates superior zero-shot performance on object recognition tasks like ImageNet.
We evaluate both vision encoders across various LLM choices and pretraining configurations.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.SSS2.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS2.SSS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS2.SSS2.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Findings.</span>
Figure <a href="#S4.F5" title="Figure 5 ‣ 4.2.1 LLM Choice ‣ 4.2 Base Models ‣ 4 Ablations: Base Models and Training ‣ Understanding the Fine-Grained Knowledge Capabilities of Vision-Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a> illustrates that the impact of substituting CLIP L/14 with DFN-CLIP H/14 depends on whether connector pretraining is performed before finetuning.
Without pretraining, DFN-CLIP degrades general VQA performance (-2.5pp) while modestly improving fine-grained benchmark scores (+2.8pp).
However, on models that have undergone connector pretraining, general VQA performance remains stable or slightly improves (+1.2pp) while fine-grained performance increases substantially (+4.5pp).
This indicates that enhanced vision encoders can significantly boost fine-grained classification performance in pretrained VLMs.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.SSS2.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent"><span class="ltx_inline-block"><svg id="S4.SS2.SSS2.p3.pic1" class="ltx_picture" height="65.96" overflow="visible" version="1.1" viewBox="0 0 550 65.96" width="550"><g style="--ltx-stroke-color:#000000;--ltx-fill-color:#000000;" fill="#000000" stroke="#000000" stroke-width="0.4pt" transform="translate(0,65.96) matrix(1 0 0 -1 0 0)"><g style="--ltx-fill-color:#404040;" fill="#404040" fill-opacity="1.0"><path style="stroke:none" d="M 0 5.91 L 0 60.06 C 0 63.32 2.64 65.96 5.91 65.96 L 544.09 65.96 C 547.36 65.96 550 63.32 550 60.06 L 550 5.91 C 550 2.64 547.36 0 544.09 0 L 5.91 0 C 2.64 0 0 2.64 0 5.91 Z"></path></g><g style="--ltx-fill-color:#F2F2F2;" fill="#F2F2F2" fill-opacity="1.0"><path style="stroke:none" d="M 1.97 5.91 L 1.97 60.06 C 1.97 62.23 3.73 63.99 5.91 63.99 L 544.09 63.99 C 546.27 63.99 548.03 62.23 548.03 60.06 L 548.03 5.91 C 548.03 3.73 546.27 1.97 544.09 1.97 L 5.91 1.97 C 3.73 1.97 1.97 3.73 1.97 5.91 Z"></path></g><g fill-opacity="1.0" transform="matrix(1.0 0.0 0.0 1.0 21.65 13.78)"><foreignObject style="--ltx-fo-width:36.62em;--ltx-fo-height:2.78em;--ltx-fo-depth:0em;font-size:10pt;" height="38.4" overflow="visible" transform="matrix(1 0 0 -1 0 38.4)" width="506.72"><span class="ltx_foreignobject_container"><span class="ltx_foreignobject_content"><span id="S4.SS2.SSS2.p3.pic1.1" class="ltx_inline-sectional-block ltx_minipage">
                      
<section id="S4.SS2.SSS2.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_font_bold ltx_font_italic ltx_title_paragraph" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">Takeaway 2:</h5>

<span id="S4.SS2.SSS2.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<span id="S4.SS2.SSS2.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS2.SSS2.Px1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">Better vision encoders (like DFN-CLIP vs. CLIP) in VLMs improve fine-grained classification, but only when these encoders are properly integrated through pretraining before the finetuning stage.</span></span>
</span>
</section>
                    </span></span></span></foreignObject></g></g></svg></span>
</div>
<figure id="S4.F7" class="ltx_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_2">
<figure id="S4.F7.fig1" class="ltx_figure ltx_figure_panel ltx_minipage ltx_align_center ltx_align_middle" style="width:190.8pt;"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2602.17871v1/pt_ablation.svg" id="S4.F7.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:264/176;" width="264" height="176"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 6: </span><span id="S4.F7.fig1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Ablating pretraining data.</span> Adding either LLaVA (CC-3M) or Molmo (PixMo-Cap) data gives similar gains. LLaVA data increases fine-grained and general scores by +4.0pp and +2.1pp respectively, while PixMo data increases them by +2.4pp and +2.5pp.</figcaption>
</figure></div><div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_2">
<figure id="S4.F7.fig2" class="ltx_figure ltx_figure_panel ltx_minipage ltx_align_center ltx_align_middle" style="width:190.8pt;"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2602.17871v1/ptstyle_ablation.svg" id="S4.F7.g2" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:264/176;" width="264" height="176"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 7: </span><span id="S4.F7.fig2.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Ablating training method, comparing connector-only pretraining with LLM+connector tuning.</span> Unfreezing the LLM during pretraining yields a +5.5pp improvement in fine-grained performance without adversely affecting general VQA scores.</figcaption>
</figure></div></div>
</figure>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.3 </span>Training Methods</h3>

<div id="S4.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Recent VLMs are typically trained in two stages <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib26" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liu et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib44" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2024b</a>; <a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chen et al., 2024c</a>)</cite>. The first stage, pretraining, involves training on large-scale image-caption datasets using a captioning task to establish alignment between the vision encoder and LLM. The second stage, instruction tuning, refines the VLM with carefully curated multi-round, multi-modal instruction completion data, aligning it with human intent for real-world applications. Here, we explore the impact of these two training stages on the fine-grained capabilities of VLMs.</p>
</div>
<section id="S4.SS3.SSS1" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">4.3.1 </span>Pretraining</h4>

<figure id="S4.T1" class="ltx_table">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 1: </span><span id="S4.T1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Summary of important ablation settings and comparison to existing models (bolded).</span> Upgrading the base LLM and vision encoder, as well as pretraining the connector and LLM on sufficient data, provide benefits to fine-grained performance, while instruction finetuning has a smaller effect. This is in contrast to general VQA benchmarks, where choice of LLM plays a larger part.</figcaption>

<td id="S4.T1.4.5.5" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center" style="padding:0.5pt 5.0pt;"><span id="S4.T1.4.5.5.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-bg-color:#EBEBEB;">LLaVA</span></td>

<td id="S4.T1.4.5.7" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center" style="padding:0.5pt 5.0pt;"><span id="S4.T1.4.5.7.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-bg-color:#EBEBEB;">57.9 (+5.1)</span></td>
<td id="S4.T1.4.5.8" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center" style="padding:0.5pt 5.0pt;"><span id="S4.T1.4.5.8.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-bg-color:#EBEBEB;">41.2 (+1.9)</span></td></tr>
<tr id="S4.T1.4.6" class="ltx_tr" style="--ltx-bg-color:#FFFFFF;">
<td id="S4.T1.4.6.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_border_r" style="padding:0.5pt 5.0pt;"><span id="S4.T1.4.6.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-bg-color:#FFFFFF;">Qwen2 LLM</span></td>
