</figure>
<div id="S4.SS3.SSS1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS3.SSS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS3.SSS1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Setup.</span>
We investigate several critical questions about the pretraining process:</p>
<ul id="S4.I1" class="ltx_itemize">
<li id="S4.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S4.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Is pretraining necessary for LLaVA-architecture models when the base models are already pretrained on billion-scale data?</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S4.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S4.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">How does connector-only pretraining compare with unfreezing the LLM?</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S4.I1.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S4.I1.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.I1.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">How important is the quality of pretraining data for downstream performance?</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS3.SSS1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS3.SSS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">We experiment with three pretraining configurations: LLaVA pretraining data <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib26" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liu et al., 2023</a>)</cite> (a subset of CC-3M with web-scraped captions), Molmo pretraining data <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib47" title="" class="ltx_ref">Deitke et al., 2024</a>)</cite> (PixMo-Cap, with high-quality human-annotated detailed captions), and no pretraining.
For most experiments, we pretrain only the connector following <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib26" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liu et al. (2023)</a></cite>.
Additionally, we explore a strategy similar to <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib47" title="" class="ltx_ref">Deitke et al. (2024)</a></cite>, where we pretrain the connector for 20% of the steps before unfreezing the LLM for the remaining 80%.
All configurations are followed by one epoch of finetuning on LLaVA finetuning data.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS3.SSS1.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS3.SSS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS3.SSS1.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Findings.</span>
Figure <a href="#S4.F7" title="Figure 7 ‣ 4.2.2 Vision Encoder Choice ‣ 4.2 Base Models ‣ 4 Ablations: Base Models and Training ‣ Understanding the Fine-Grained Knowledge Capabilities of Vision-Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">7</span></a> illustrates our pretraining ablation results.
We observe that connector-only pretraining generally enhances VLM performance, with the exception of the Qwen2 and CLIP ViT-L/14 combination.
The benefits are particularly substantial for Vicuna-based VLMs, which show an average improvement of +6.1pp in fine-grained classification and +3.1pp in general VQA performance.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS3.SSS1.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent"><span class="ltx_inline-block"><svg id="S4.SS3.SSS1.p4.pic1" class="ltx_picture" height="65.19" overflow="visible" version="1.1" viewBox="0 0 550 65.19" width="550"><g style="--ltx-stroke-color:#000000;--ltx-fill-color:#000000;" fill="#000000" stroke="#000000" stroke-width="0.4pt" transform="translate(0,65.19) matrix(1 0 0 -1 0 0)"><g style="--ltx-fill-color:#404040;" fill="#404040" fill-opacity="1.0"><path style="stroke:none" d="M 0 5.91 L 0 59.29 C 0 62.55 2.64 65.19 5.91 65.19 L 544.09 65.19 C 547.36 65.19 550 62.55 550 59.29 L 550 5.91 C 550 2.64 547.36 0 544.09 0 L 5.91 0 C 2.64 0 0 2.64 0 5.91 Z"></path></g><g style="--ltx-fill-color:#F2F2F2;" fill="#F2F2F2" fill-opacity="1.0"><path style="stroke:none" d="M 1.97 5.91 L 1.97 59.29 C 1.97 61.46 3.73 63.22 5.91 63.22 L 544.09 63.22 C 546.27 63.22 548.03 61.46 548.03 59.29 L 548.03 5.91 C 548.03 3.73 546.27 1.97 544.09 1.97 L 5.91 1.97 C 3.73 1.97 1.97 3.73 1.97 5.91 Z"></path></g><g fill-opacity="1.0" transform="matrix(1.0 0.0 0.0 1.0 21.65 13.78)"><foreignObject style="--ltx-fo-width:36.62em;--ltx-fo-height:2.72em;--ltx-fo-depth:0em;font-size:10pt;" height="37.63" overflow="visible" transform="matrix(1 0 0 -1 0 37.63)" width="506.72"><span class="ltx_foreignobject_container"><span class="ltx_foreignobject_content"><span id="S4.SS3.SSS1.p4.pic1.1" class="ltx_inline-sectional-block ltx_minipage">
                      
<section id="S4.SS3.SSS1.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_font_bold ltx_font_italic ltx_title_paragraph" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">Takeaway 3:</h5>

<span id="S4.SS3.SSS1.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<span id="S4.SS3.SSS1.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS3.SSS1.Px1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">Large-scale pretraining on image captioning datasets substantially improves fine-grained classification performance but has a more modest effect on general VLM benchmarks.</span></span>
</span>
</section>
                    </span></span></span></foreignObject></g></g></svg></span>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS3.SSS1.p5" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS3.SSS1.p5.1" class="ltx_p">Surprisingly, we find minimal differences between pretraining on low-quality web-scraped captions (LLaVA) versus highly detailed human annotations (PixMo). Compared to LLaVA data, PixMo data results in a -1.6pp change in fine-grained performance and a +0.4pp change in general VQA scores.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS3.SSS1.p6" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent"><span class="ltx_inline-block"><svg id="S4.SS3.SSS1.p6.pic1" class="ltx_picture" height="48.59" overflow="visible" version="1.1" viewBox="0 0 550 48.59" width="550"><g style="--ltx-stroke-color:#000000;--ltx-fill-color:#000000;" fill="#000000" stroke="#000000" stroke-width="0.4pt" transform="translate(0,48.59) matrix(1 0 0 -1 0 0)"><g style="--ltx-fill-color:#404040;" fill="#404040" fill-opacity="1.0"><path style="stroke:none" d="M 0 5.91 L 0 42.68 C 0 45.94 2.64 48.59 5.91 48.59 L 544.09 48.59 C 547.36 48.59 550 45.94 550 42.68 L 550 5.91 C 550 2.64 547.36 0 544.09 0 L 5.91 0 C 2.64 0 0 2.64 0 5.91 Z"></path></g><g style="--ltx-fill-color:#F2F2F2;" fill="#F2F2F2" fill-opacity="1.0"><path style="stroke:none" d="M 1.97 5.91 L 1.97 42.68 C 1.97 44.86 3.73 46.62 5.91 46.62 L 544.09 46.62 C 546.27 46.62 548.03 44.86 548.03 42.68 L 548.03 5.91 C 548.03 3.73 546.27 1.97 544.09 1.97 L 5.91 1.97 C 3.73 1.97 1.97 3.73 1.97 5.91 Z"></path></g><g fill-opacity="1.0" transform="matrix(1.0 0.0 0.0 1.0 21.65 13.78)"><foreignObject style="--ltx-fo-width:36.62em;--ltx-fo-height:1.52em;--ltx-fo-depth:0em;font-size:10pt;" height="21.03" overflow="visible" transform="matrix(1 0 0 -1 0 21.03)" width="506.72"><span class="ltx_foreignobject_container"><span class="ltx_foreignobject_content"><span id="S4.SS3.SSS1.p6.pic1.1" class="ltx_inline-sectional-block ltx_minipage">
                      
<section id="S4.SS3.SSS1.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_font_bold ltx_font_italic ltx_title_paragraph" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">Takeaway 4:</h5>

<span id="S4.SS3.SSS1.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<span id="S4.SS3.SSS1.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS3.SSS1.Px2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">Pretraining data quality has a limited impact on overall model performance.</span></span>
</span>
</section>
                    </span></span></span></foreignObject></g></g></svg></span>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS3.SSS1.p7" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS3.SSS1.p7.1" class="ltx_p">We hypothesize that connector-only pretraining may prevent the model from fully leveraging higher-quality captions.
To test this hypothesis, we experiment with pretraining both the LLM and connector, incorporating a 20% connector-only warmup phase.
Figure <a href="#S4.F7" title="Figure 7 ‣ 4.2.2 Vision Encoder Choice ‣ 4.2 Base Models ‣ 4 Ablations: Base Models and Training ‣ Understanding the Fine-Grained Knowledge Capabilities of Vision-Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">7</span></a> shows that this approach significantly enhances fine-grained classification performance (+5.5pp) without compromising general VQA scores.
However, this improvement occurs with both LLaVA and PixMo pretraining data, suggesting that training on the lower-quality captions does not impair the LLM’s language capabilities.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS3.SSS1.p8" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent"><span class="ltx_inline-block"><svg id="S4.SS3.SSS1.p8.pic1" class="ltx_picture" height="48.59" overflow="visible" version="1.1" viewBox="0 0 550 48.59" width="550"><g style="--ltx-stroke-color:#000000;--ltx-fill-color:#000000;" fill="#000000" stroke="#000000" stroke-width="0.4pt" transform="translate(0,48.59) matrix(1 0 0 -1 0 0)"><g style="--ltx-fill-color:#404040;" fill="#404040" fill-opacity="1.0"><path style="stroke:none" d="M 0 5.91 L 0 42.68 C 0 45.94 2.64 48.59 5.91 48.59 L 544.09 48.59 C 547.36 48.59 550 45.94 550 42.68 L 550 5.91 C 550 2.64 547.36 0 544.09 0 L 5.91 0 C 2.64 0 0 2.64 0 5.91 Z"></path></g><g style="--ltx-fill-color:#F2F2F2;" fill="#F2F2F2" fill-opacity="1.0"><path style="stroke:none" d="M 1.97 5.91 L 1.97 42.68 C 1.97 44.86 3.73 46.62 5.91 46.62 L 544.09 46.62 C 546.27 46.62 548.03 44.86 548.03 42.68 L 548.03 5.91 C 548.03 3.73 546.27 1.97 544.09 1.97 L 5.91 1.97 C 3.73 1.97 1.97 3.73 1.97 5.91 Z"></path></g><g fill-opacity="1.0" transform="matrix(1.0 0.0 0.0 1.0 21.65 13.78)"><foreignObject style="--ltx-fo-width:36.62em;--ltx-fo-height:1.52em;--ltx-fo-depth:0em;font-size:10pt;" height="21.03" overflow="visible" transform="matrix(1 0 0 -1 0 21.03)" width="506.72"><span class="ltx_foreignobject_container"><span class="ltx_foreignobject_content"><span id="S4.SS3.SSS1.p8.pic1.1" class="ltx_inline-sectional-block ltx_minipage">
                      
<section id="S4.SS3.SSS1.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_font_bold ltx_font_italic ltx_title_paragraph" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">Takeaway 5:</h5>

<span id="S4.SS3.SSS1.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<span id="S4.SS3.SSS1.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS3.SSS1.Px3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">Pretraining both LLM and connector substantially enhances fine-grained benchmark performance while maintaining general VQA scores.</span></span>
</span>
</section>
                    </span></span></span></foreignObject></g></g></svg></span>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS3.SSS2" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">4.3.2 </span>Finetuning</h4>

<figure id="S4.F8" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2602.17871v1/ablation_progress.svg" id="S4.F8.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:302/201;" width="302" height="201"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 8: </span><span id="S4.F8.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Progression of combined ablation effects.</span> Starting with Vicuna-7B and CLIP ViT-L/14, we progressively modify the base LLM, vision encoder, and training settings to increase fine-grained classification accuracy from 52.8% to 73.4%, accounting for more than half the gap to Qwen2-VL-Chat’s 87.9%. We attribute the remaining performance difference primarily to Qwen2-VL’s extensive pretraining data of 1.4T tokens.</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S4.SS3.SSS2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS3.SSS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS3.SSS2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Setup.</span>
Departing from our previous setup, we begin with the pretrained Qwen2-VL-7B-Base model <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib44" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2024b</a>)</cite> (from which Qwen2-VL-7B-Chat is trained) and finetune on LLaVA-Instruct data <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib26" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liu et al., 2023</a>)</cite> following our earlier experimental protocol.
We compare these results with Qwen2-VL-7B-Chat, which employs 2M in-house examples for instruction finetuning <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib44" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2024b</a>)</cite>.
This comparison helps isolate the effects of different finetuning datasets.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS3.SSS2.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS3.SSS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS3.SSS2.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Findings.</span>
Our results indicate that finetuning solely on LLaVA finetuning data slightly reduces both fine-grained and general benchmark performance.
Specifically, fine-grained scores decrease by 2.4pp (from 87.9% to 85.5%), while general benchmark scores drop by 1.3pp (from 62.4% to 61.1%).
As illustrated in Figure <a href="#S4.F8" title="Figure 8 ‣ 4.3.2 Finetuning ‣ 4.3 Training Methods ‣ 4 Ablations: Base Models and Training ‣ Understanding the Fine-Grained Knowledge Capabilities of Vision-Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">8</span></a>, this represents the smallest contribution to fine-grained performance across all our ablations, suggesting that instruction finetuning plays a less critical role in fine-grained knowledge acquisition compared to base model selection and pretraining strategy.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS3.SSS2.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent"><span class="ltx_inline-block"><svg id="S4.SS3.SSS2.p3.pic1" class="ltx_picture" height="48.59" overflow="visible" version="1.1" viewBox="0 0 550 48.59" width="550"><g style="--ltx-stroke-color:#000000;--ltx-fill-color:#000000;" fill="#000000" stroke="#000000" stroke-width="0.4pt" transform="translate(0,48.59) matrix(1 0 0 -1 0 0)"><g style="--ltx-fill-color:#404040;" fill="#404040" fill-opacity="1.0"><path style="stroke:none" d="M 0 5.91 L 0 42.68 C 0 45.94 2.64 48.59 5.91 48.59 L 544.09 48.59 C 547.36 48.59 550 45.94 550 42.68 L 550 5.91 C 550 2.64 547.36 0 544.09 0 L 5.91 0 C 2.64 0 0 2.64 0 5.91 Z"></path></g><g style="--ltx-fill-color:#F2F2F2;" fill="#F2F2F2" fill-opacity="1.0"><path style="stroke:none" d="M 1.97 5.91 L 1.97 42.68 C 1.97 44.86 3.73 46.62 5.91 46.62 L 544.09 46.62 C 546.27 46.62 548.03 44.86 548.03 42.68 L 548.03 5.91 C 548.03 3.73 546.27 1.97 544.09 1.97 L 5.91 1.97 C 3.73 1.97 1.97 3.73 1.97 5.91 Z"></path></g><g fill-opacity="1.0" transform="matrix(1.0 0.0 0.0 1.0 21.65 13.78)"><foreignObject style="--ltx-fo-width:36.62em;--ltx-fo-height:1.52em;--ltx-fo-depth:0em;font-size:10pt;" height="21.03" overflow="visible" transform="matrix(1 0 0 -1 0 21.03)" width="506.72"><span class="ltx_foreignobject_container"><span class="ltx_foreignobject_content"><span id="S4.SS3.SSS2.p3.pic1.1" class="ltx_inline-sectional-block ltx_minipage">
                      
<section id="S4.SS3.SSS2.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_font_bold ltx_font_italic ltx_title_paragraph" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">Takeaway 6:</h5>

<span id="S4.SS3.SSS2.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<span id="S4.SS3.SSS2.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS3.SSS2.Px1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">The instruction finetuning stage has comparatively less impact on fine-grained classification performance than other factors.</span></span>
</span>
</section>
                    </span></span></span></foreignObject></g></g></svg></span>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS4" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.4 </span>Summary of Ablations</h3>

<div id="S4.SS4.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Figure <a href="#S4.F8" title="Figure 8 ‣ 4.3.2 Finetuning ‣ 4.3 Training Methods ‣ 4 Ablations: Base Models and Training ‣ Understanding the Fine-Grained Knowledge Capabilities of Vision-Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">8</span></a> and Table <a href="#S4.T1" title="Table 1 ‣ 4.3.1 Pretraining ‣ 4.3 Training Methods ‣ 4 Ablations: Base Models and Training ‣ Understanding the Fine-Grained Knowledge Capabilities of Vision-Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a> synthesize our ablation studies, showing how each component contributes to closing the performance gap between the weakest and strongest VLMs on both fine-grained and general VQA tasks.
Beginning with the baseline LLaVA architecture <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib26" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liu et al., 2023</a>)</cite> (Vicuna-7B <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chiang et al., 2023</a>)</cite> and CLIP ViT-L/14 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">Radford et al., 2021</a>)</cite>), we systematically modified various components to increase fine-grained performance from 52.8% to 73.4%, and general VQA performance from 39.3% to 49.9%.
This analysis reveals that switching to DFN-CLIP <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib49" title="" class="ltx_ref">Fang et al., 2023</a>)</cite> and unfreezing the LLM during pretraining disproportionately enhances fine-grained capabilities compared to general VLM abilities, whereas switching the LLM to Qwen2-7B <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib29" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yang et al., 2024</a>)</cite> accounts for most of the increase in general VQA performance.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS4.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS4.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Despite these substantial improvements, a notable 12-point gap in fine-grained classification performance remains unexplained by our ablations (Table <a href="#S4.T1" title="Table 1 ‣ 4.3.1 Pretraining ‣ 4.3 Training Methods ‣ 4 Ablations: Base Models and Training ‣ Understanding the Fine-Grained Knowledge Capabilities of Vision-Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>).
We consider two potential factors to account for this discrepancy: architectural differences and pretraining data scale.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS4.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS4.p3.1" class="ltx_p">While architectural changes could contribute to performance differences, our observational results (Section <a href="#S3.SS4" title="3.4 Results ‣ 3 Evaluation: Fine-grained Classification ‣ Understanding the Fine-Grained Knowledge Capabilities of Vision-Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.4</span></a>) and training ablations (Section <a href="#S4.SS3" title="4.3 Training Methods ‣ 4 Ablations: Base Models and Training ‣ Understanding the Fine-Grained Knowledge Capabilities of Vision-Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.3</span></a>) strongly suggest that pretraining data scale is the dominant factor.
Our experiments with LLaVA <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib26" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liu et al., 2023</a>)</cite> and PixMo <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib47" title="" class="ltx_ref">Deitke et al., 2024</a>)</cite> data involved relatively small datasets—each comprising fewer than 1M images and captions, or approximately 200M and 400M tokens, respectively.
In contrast, <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib44" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al. (2024b)</a></cite> report pretraining Qwen2-VL on an extensive 1.4T tokens—orders of magnitude more than in our experiments.
This substantial disparity in pretraining data scale likely accounts for the remaining performance gap, highlighting the critical role of extensive pretraining in developing VLMs with superior fine-grained classification capabilities.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S5" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">5 </span>Limitations &amp; Conclusion</h2>

<div id="S5.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Our study has some practical limitations that open up opportunities for future research.
Due to computational constraints, we could only compare training on &lt;1M data points rather than the billion (B) scale training utilized by some newer VLMs, leaving open the question of how large-scale training might impact our observations.
Additionally, newer work suggest different pretraining strategies, which might interact differently with fine-grained visual understanding.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.p2.1" class="ltx_p">In this work, we systematically evaluate state-of-the-art vision-language models (VLMs) on fine-grained classification benchmarks, highlighting fine-grained visual classification as a crucial yet underexplored dimension of VLMs. Through an in-depth analysis of key model components and training paradigms, we provide insights into strategies for improving fine-grained classification and enhancing vision-centric capabilities, ultimately strengthening the applicability of VLMs in real-world scenarios that demand precise visual understanding.</p>
</div>
</section>

<section id="A2" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix B </span>Evaluation</h2>

<section id="A2.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">B.1 </span>Fine-grained classification</h3>

<div id="A2.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A2.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">As covered in Section <a href="#S3.SS2" title="3.2 Benchmarks ‣ 3 Evaluation: Fine-grained Classification ‣ Understanding the Fine-Grained Knowledge Capabilities of Vision-Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.2</span></a>, we evaluate VLMs and base vision encoders on four different traditional classification benchmarks:</p>
</div>
<div id="A2.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A2.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A2.SS1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">ImageNet-1K</span> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib25" title="" class="ltx_ref">Deng et al., 2009</a>)</cite>:
A foundational image classification dataset covering a broad range of supercategories, each containing multiple fine-grained subcategories, based on the WordNet hierarchy.
The ImageNet test set contains 50,000 images with classification across 1,000 classes.</p>
</div>
<div id="A2.SS1.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A2.SS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">However, because of the nature of the ImageNet/WordNet class hierarchy, there are many classes which are too visually distinct from other classes to create hard multiple choice examples for (for instance, there are only three classes under the “person” category).
Due to this drawback, in addition to the excessive size of the dataset, we employ human annotated incorrect model predictions from <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib24" title="" class="ltx_ref">Recht et al. (2019)</a></cite> to select images for which hard negative answer choices can be constructed.
Starting with 19,056 annotated examples, we narrow down the pool to 5,457 images consisting of 928 different classes out of the original 1,000.
Furthermore, since this test example curation leaves the remaining classes unevenly balanced, we report the mean-per-class accuracy for ImageNet.</p>
</div>
<div id="A2.SS1.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A2.SS1.p4.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A2.SS1.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Oxford Flowers-102</span> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">Nilsback and Zisserman, 2008</a>)</cite>:
A dataset of 102 flower species characterized by high intra-class variation and inter-class similarity.
The Flowers dataset consists of 6,149 test examples.</p>
</div>
<div id="A2.SS1.p5" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A2.SS1.p5.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A2.SS1.p5.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Oxford-IIIT Pet-37</span> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">Parkhi et al., 2012</a>)</cite>:
A collection of 37 pet categories with challenging variations in pose, lighting, and occlusion.
The Pets dataset consists of 3,669 test examples.</p>
</div>
<div id="A2.SS1.p6" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A2.SS1.p6.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A2.SS1.p6.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Food-101</span> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">Bossard et al., 2014</a>)</cite>:
A dataset comprising 101 food categories, exhibiting substantial visual diversity within each class.
The Food dataset consists of 25,250 test examples.</p>
</div>
<div id="A2.SS1.p7" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A2.SS1.p7.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A2.SS1.p7.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Question generation.</span>
For all fine-grained classification test sets except the ImageNet dataset (described above), we generate hard negatives by performing zero-shot classification on the test examples using an OpenCLIP ViT-L/14 trained on LAION <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">Schuhmann et al., 2022</a>)</cite>, following <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">Geigle et al. (2024)</a></cite>.
We take the top 4 predictions that are incorrect, and shuffle them with the correct label to produce the list of answer choices.</p>
</div>
<div id="A2.SS1.p8" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A2.SS1.p8.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A2.SS1.p8.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Prompt formatting.</span>
In our multiple choice VQA format, the question is always of the form “What type of object is in this photo?”
The answer choices are formatted as “A. Option 1\n B. Option 2\n C. Option 3\n D. Option 4\n E. Option 5”.
However, since different VLMs are trained with different multiple choice prompts and format, we use each model’s corresponding format from VLMEvalKit <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">Duan et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, for instance: “Answer with the option’s letter from the given choices directly.”</p>
</div>
<div id="A2.SS1.p9" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A2.SS1.p9.1" class="ltx_p">For CLIP models, we use the standard zero-shot evaluation procedure, and thus there is no question format.
The classnames passed to the text encoder are instead formatted in the template of “a photo of a {classname}”.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A2.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">B.2 </span>General VQA</h3>

<div id="A2.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A2.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In our initial observational testing from Section <a href="#S3" title="3 Evaluation: Fine-grained Classification ‣ Understanding the Fine-Grained Knowledge Capabilities of Vision-Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>, we rely directly on the numbers reported on the OpenVLM Leaderboard <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">Duan et al., 2024</a>)</cite>.
The default leaderboard reports the average score across eight diverse VLM benchmarks:
MMBench <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib31" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liu et al., 2024b</a>)</cite>, MMStar <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib41" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chen et al., 2024b</a>)</cite>, MMMU (Val) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib43" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yue et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, MathVista <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib42" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lu et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, OCRBench <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liu et al., 2024c</a>)</cite>, AI2D <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib40" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kembhavi et al., 2016</a>)</cite>, HallusionBench <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">Guan et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, and MMVet <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib38" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yu et al., 2024</a>)</cite>.
This reported average score is used only in Figure <a href="#S3.F3" title="Figure 3 ‣ 3.4 Results ‣ 3 Evaluation: Fine-grained Classification ‣ Understanding the Fine-Grained Knowledge Capabilities of Vision-Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a> in our paper.</p>
</div>
<div id="A2.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A2.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">For all further evaluations, both on existing models and our own models trained in Section <a href="#S4" title="4 Ablations: Base Models and Training ‣ Understanding the Fine-Grained Knowledge Capabilities of Vision-Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>, we narrow this down to a subset of multiple-choice VLM benchmarks for a more direct comparison of performance.
Specifically, we evaluate VLMs on three benchmarks:</p>
</div>
<div id="A2.SS2.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A2.SS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A2.SS2.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">MMBench</span> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib31" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liu et al., 2024b</a>)</cite>:
A dataset of 2,948 examples testing a wide range of VLM capabilities split between perception and reasoning.
While the majority of the examples deal with coarse-grained perception and visual reasoning tasks, some examples test “fine-grained perception”, though the categories (such as action recognition, attribute recognition, and OCR) are in a different domain from the fine-grained classification datasets we consider.</p>
</div>
<div id="A2.SS2.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A2.SS2.p4.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A2.SS2.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">MMMU (Val)</span> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib43" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yue et al., 2024</a>)</cite>:
A large-scale multimodal dataset covering a wide distribution of domains and applications.
Though the test set has 10,500 examples, most works cite model performance on the validation split, which contains 900 questions.
MMMU tests general knowledge tied to visual perception across art, science, engineering, medicine, business, and humanities.</p>
</div>
<div id="A2.SS2.p5" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A2.SS2.p5.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A2.SS2.p5.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">MMStar</span> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib41" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chen et al., 2024b</a>)</cite>:
A dataset comprised of 1,500 questions selected by human annotators.
The examples are chosen to cover a diverse set of tasks, both across domain and low-level model capabilities.</p>
</div>
<div id="A2.SS2.p6" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A2.SS2.p6.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A2.SS2.p6.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Evaluation procedure.</span>
For the general VQA benchmarks, we defer entirely to the VLMEvalKit evaluation code <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">Duan et al., 2024</a>)</cite>.
All existing models have a pre-defined evaluation procedure, and for our own trained models, we apply the LLaVA evaluation code, since we exclusively finetune on LLaVA-Instruct data.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="A3" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix C </span>Training</h2>

<div id="A3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We build on the LLaVA-1.5 training codebase <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib26" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liu et al., 2023</a>)</cite>.
For the majority of experiments, we stick to the LLaVA architecture and training procedure.</p>
</div>
<div id="A3.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A3.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A3.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Pretraining.</span>
This means one epoch of pretraining on the LLaVA pretraining data, obtained from CC-3M images and captions, or Molmo pretraining data (PixMo-Cap).
For PixMo-Cap, we only use the “caption” field and not the raw audio transcript.
During pretraining, we use a batch size of 256.
In most of our pretraining runs, we tune only the randomly-initialized MLP connector with a learning rate of 1e-3.
When ablating pretraining strategy, we first tune the connector only as warmup, for 20% of steps, then unfreeze the LLM and tune it as well, with a learning rate of 2e-5 for the remaining 80% of steps.</p>
</div>
<div id="A3.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A3.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A3.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Finetuning.</span>
For finetuning, we always train for one epoch on the LLaVA-1.5 finetuning data, which consists of LLaVA-Instruct and VQA training data from various datasets to allow proper benchmarking.
During finetuning, we maintain a learning rate of 2e-5 for the LLM, with a batch size of 128.
The vision encoder remains frozen during both phases of training.</p>
</div>
<div id="A3.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A3.p4.1" class="ltx_p">For the ablation experiment on the Qwen2-VL architecture, we start with Qwen2-VL-7B Base and train with the same method, unfreezing only the LLM.</p>
</div>
<div id="A3.p5" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A3.p5.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A3.p5.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Compute.</span>
We train all models using 4 nodes of 4 A100 (40GB) GPUs each.
Training typically completes within 20 hours, with variation depending on the CLIP model size.</p>
</div>
<div id="A3.p6" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A3.p6.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A3.p6.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">LLaVA vs. PixMo data.</span>
In our main text, we refer to the difference in caption quality between LLaVA pretraining data and PixMo pretraining data.
LLaVA pretraining data is sourced from CC-3M, which consists of web-scraped captions, commonly known for low quality and relevance.
PixMo-Cap is, on the other hand, collected from human annotators recording a 60–90 second audio description of an image, and then combined into a proper image caption <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib47" title="" class="ltx_ref">Deitke et al., 2024</a>)</cite>.
A surface analysis of the two datasets shows that the LLaVA data averages 9.8 words per caption, whereas the PixMo data averages 169 words per caption.</p>
</div>
<div id="A3.p7" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A3.p7.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A3.p7.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">LLaVA caption example:</span>
“front panel bracket cover for suzuki”</p>
</div>
<div id="A3.p8" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A3.p8.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A3.p8.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">PixMo caption example:</span>
“The poster from the TV show ”Law and Order” features a past cast ensemble set in an interrogation room. On the left is a Hispanic man, identified as Detective Nick Amaro, portrayed by Danny Pino. He has dark hair, olive skin, and is dressed in a gray jacket, blue shirt, and black tie. Standing beside him is a blonde woman with shoulder-length hair, who is identified as Detective Amanda Rollins, played by Kelli Giddish. She is … The backdrop is an interrogation room, with a concrete wall and a portion of a two-way mirror visible, adding to the procedural drama’s atmospheric setting.”</p>
</div>
</section>
</article>
